1 · Vision
Designers make bol specific
By 2028, every designer at bol works as a maker, because making something real, on real data and with real users, is how we add what AI can't (the specific) and use what it can (speed).
Shows
Artefacts for dialogue
Turns an idea into something working, on real data, in days. bol decides on evidence, with less rework and a faster path to a validated decision.
Discovers
Time back for discovery
AI makes building cheap for everyone, so bol can't win on speed alone. Deciding what's worth building, and shaping agents people trust, is what keeps bol distinct.
Unites
Blurred lines but never alone
Works alongside product, engineering and data: the artefact is how the crafts think together. Fewer handoffs, and decisions in days instead of sprints.

Risk
Shorter cycles mean more context switching and more cognitive load.
Mitigation: Fewer parallel cycles per person, protected discovery time, and load tracked next to satisfaction.
AI only gives time back if we invest first
Time back takes investment first: a design language, guardrails and sharper intent. Without it, time goes into reviewing output. With it, time goes into discovery.

1 · Vision
Three shifts in how the craft works
Screens → Intent
Most early effort goes here: guardrails and context that make output good enough to trust.
How we get there
→ Design language as rules agents can read
→ Skills that teach the tools how bol designs
→ Real context: research, data, past decisions
→ Evals from real good and bad examples
→ Iterate until the rejection rate is acceptable
Risk
For some time, building the system eats the time it should free.
Handoffs → Dialogue
A working thing on real data changes the quality of the decision.
How we get there
→ Working prototypes, not static screens
→ A safe sandbox on the real pipeline and code
→ Access to repos, tools and real data
→ Three-minute demos replace handoff decks
Risk
People changing code they don't fully understand.
Domains → Journeys
Designers own journeys across domains, with product. Domains keep their systems.
How we get there
→ One cross-domain journey squad. 
→ A cross-domain designer council owns the standards
→ Change structures only after the pilot shows it works
Risk
Journey ownership clashes with domain accountability.

1 · Vision · Unspoken Diary, 2026
From idea to live product, in 8 hours
A photo diary for the Unspoken Summit. Each attendee gets a secret lens and one photo a day for three days, in a mobile view; the facilitator runs the room from a desktop view on the projector. On the last day the room guesses each other's lens using John Berger's theory. I designed it and took it live with Claude Code, without deep code knowledge.

2 · Standards & frameworks
Four behaviours are the new standard
In an AI-first craft, the standard is how people work
Tools will change every quarter, and behaviours decide whether any tool produces good work. So the first standard I'd introduce is four behaviours, co-written with designers, researchers and writers, then made practical through one way of working.
Universal vs local: the behaviours are the same everywhere, and how they show up is local. A partner-tools designer and a consumer designer will use different evidence and different data.
High agency
High taste
High curiosity
High adaptability

2 · Standards & frameworks
Each behaviour is observable, and bol owes something back
Behaviour
What it looks like
How we make it possible
High agency
solves it without waiting
Builds a working prototype on real data to test a hypothesis, instead of asking for resources first. Brings a proposal with the problem.
What it's not: Taking ownership and credit, and forgetting the team that made it possible.
→ Access to tools, repositories and data
→ A dedicated prototyping environment
→ Permission to run small experiments autonomously
High taste
knows what good looks like, and why
Rejects plausible but generic output and can explain why. Writes intent agents can use. Knows what to remove.
What it's not: personal preference, or pixel policing.
→ A shared design language that captures intent
→ Critiques built on real examples
→ Time to study the best work in and outside e-commerce
High curiosity
reaches for the tool before the expert
Tries the new tool or workflow first, and shares where it failed. Goes looking for data and user evidence.
What it's not: chasing every new tool.
→ Protected time to explore
→ An open craft lab to share findings
High adaptability
changes course when the evidence says so
Changes their mind in public. Works across crafts when the work needs it. Comfortable moving between many topics.
What it's not: no direction, or constant pivoting.
→ Short cycles with exit criteria agreed upfront
→ Psychological safety to be wrong

2 · Standards & frameworks
One loop turns the behaviours into daily work
The maker loop
Frame
Explore
Make
Decide
Encode
Observe
owns the problem and the hypothesis
AI as auditor: edge cases, gaps, simulated users
a working thing, on real data
judges the evidence, decision documented
intent into the design language, for agents
live behaviour, traces; change course
The behaviour that leads each step
High agency
High curiosity
High taste
High adaptability
Example: a partner agent experience
Hypothesis
Frame
What should the agent do alone, and when should it ask the partner?
Explore
Read 100 real traces and tag where it failed. Simulated partners push the edge cases.
Make
The behaviour, prototyped with a live model on real data.
Decide
Evals built from the tagged failures are the acceptance bar. The decision and its reason are written down.
Encode
Behaviour rules go into the design language: tone, how much it does alone, when it hands back. 
Observe
Traces from live conversations show whether it holds. Each failure becomes an eval example and a behaviour rule. Designers start owning how the agent behaves.
Skills we build
→ Writing behaviour specs
→ Building evals from real good and bad examples
→ Reading traces
→ Designing for trust and failure

2 · Standards & frameworks
"Quality is the hard bit" - Matthew dixit 
Defining what good UX looks like at bol is the hardest part, so the bar is written down in three layers, each with its own owner: two are universal, one stays local.
UX Basics
On-system, accessible, free of generic AI patterns
Checked by: automation that designers build
→ Designers build the automation: they write the rules and checks, tools run them on every change
→ bol's design language written into files agents read: tokens, patterns, product context
→ Tools like Impeccable flag generic AI patterns before work is merged
→ Accessibility checks built in, AI does the audit
Behaviour and Intent
Journeys hold across domains
Checked by: Design lead
→ Journeys checked across domain boundaries, edge cases and hand-overs included
→ Guards what makes bol distinct
The bar grows
From real cases: every rejection in review becomes a new rule or a test example.
Domain and User Fit
Right for this user, this data, this domain
Checked by: domain review
→ Each domain sets its own evidence: partner tools and consumer journeys differ
→ Reviews decide on working things, not decks
→ The time saved on basics goes here
What moves up
Hypothesis
Research and data decide: the same issue in three domains, or analytics showing journeys break at a domain boundary.
Universal
Local

3 · Driving change
Change without a mandate
I'd launch this change like a product, with designers as its users
The strategy is pull, not push. I go first, sharing my own tests and failures. One squad, sceptics included, proves it on real work. The crafts test it together, so it arrives as a shared position. Then each domain makes it its own. Like any craft, designers resist a change that seems to threaten the craft that made them good. So sceptics go first, because they often defend the quality bar, and people adopt what visibly makes their week better and what they helped shape.

3 · Driving change
Two actions carry the change: one in the teams, one across the crafts
Action 1
In the teams
Rituals built on bol's own beliefs
The change has to show up in designers' week.
Open craft lab
monthly · bold, curious
Findings, failures, worries. I go first.
Three-minute demos
make it happen
A working thing on real data, shown in three minutes.
Designer council
stronger together
Rotating, cross-domain, sceptics included. Co-owns the framework.
Tired from admin is not the same as tired from making something you see land. The rituals are a space to unload.
Action 2
Across the crafts
Every craft can see and try what we test.
The craft leads shape an agentic way of building software, starting with a shared test bed: new tools tested as they ship, with simulated users and real data. Every change to how we work goes through it first.
Each craft brings its part:
→ Engineering the pipeline and guardrails
→ Product the bets worth testing
→ Analytics real data, and what to measure
→ UX Research real users, where simulated ones fall short
Open question for the crafts
If making is democratised, how do our roles get redefined?
The crafts decide together where one role ends and the next begins.

3 · Driving change
Change without authority at Culligan's design evolution
A design language adopted autonomously by the product category teams, with expert support.
I owned the UX layer: who the users are, their journeys, and one UX character adapted to each context. I co-designed the touchscreen, indicator and accessibility toolkits with our agency, and approved the work.

→

Simple

Expert
→
6 Layers
On plastic and pixels
Makes it simple
One colour, one meaning
→ Azure marks critical touch points on the hardware and the filtration process on screen
→ Indicators: white all well, yellow attention, orange act now
Makes it trustworthy
Motion that tells the truth about urgency
→ Calm for steady information; pulsing only when attention is critical
→ A breathing light, so the product feels at work
Makes it expert
Rules from real use
→ 1–2 options: selecting is dispensing. 3 or more: separate steps
→ Shared office: reset to the most-used option. Home: remember the last choice

4 · Success
Behaviour first, products follow
Success in year one is designers working differently
The signals I'd watch first are behaviour and time, because they move early. Product outcomes lag two or three quarters behind, so I'd report them as they emerge, never in place of the behaviour signals. Every speed signal is paired with a quality or people signal.
The other craft leads and the UX Research Manager see the same read-outs, so UX keeps a sustained voice in how roles and teams evolve.

how designers work, and where their time goes

4 · Success · In summary
When designers work this way, bol makes better bets, faster
The strategy in three blocks, each building on the last. Stronger craft changes how teams decide, and that changes what ships: fewer wrong bets get built, less budget goes to rework, and shoppers keep choosing bol, even when every competitor has the same AI tools.

Appendix · Context for the vision
Four forces change what a designer's day is made of
Four forces, read as changes to a designer's day
The brief names four forces reshaping UX at bol. Each one changes what a designer's time is made of, and what makes a designer valuable.
What Matthew shared
A pilot is already testing two ways of working; defining what quality UX at bol looks like is "the hard bit"; and upskilling versus craft time is a tightrope.
Force (from the brief)
What it means for a designer
Engineering moves faster than design workflows
Handoffs become the bottleneck. Designers need to work where the product is built.
AI drafts the first pass of visual and interaction design
Framing and judging become the value.
AI products can't be fully mocked upfront
Designers specify behaviour as well as screens, and test it live.
New builder profiles blend design, product and engineering
Everyone makes, so someone has to hold the intent and the quality bar.
